identity.title: The Computer Does Exactly What You Say
identity.description: Give precise instructions in the correct order and predict the resulting outcome.

learning.startingState: Assumes computers understand human intentions and can fill in missing details.
learning.targetState: Understands that computers follow instructions literally in sequential order to produce outcomes.

completionCriteria: Distinguish general goals from precise instructions
Sequence dependent actions in proper order
Identify flawed instructions that produce unintended outcomes
masteryCriteria: Explain why an instruction sequence fails when a prerequisite step is out of order

content.title: Meet the World's Most Literal Assistant
content.hook: You: “Make me a sandwich.” Computer: “Sure.” It puts two slices of bread on the table and stops.
content.context: It didn't fail. You left out the instructions. The computer doesn't know what you meant—it follows the instructions you give it.
goals: See why computers need exact steps, not general goals
Arrange actions in the exact order needed to produce an outcome

content.question:
Look at this sequence:
1. Put bread on the plate.
2. Put cheese on the bread.
3. Put another piece of bread on top.

What will you have?

options.text: A plate with cheese beside the bread

content.explanation: Each instruction changes the situation step by step until the final outcome is reached.

feedback.correct: Exactly. Each step changed the situation to produce the final outcome.
feedback.incorrect: Check the three actions again. What do they produce when followed in order?

content.question: Which set gives the assistant enough information to act?

options.text: Card B: 1. Put bread on a plate. 2. Put cheese on the bread. 3. Put bread on the cheese.

content.explanation: Computers cannot read minds or interpret goals. They need physical, step-by-step actions.

feedback.correct: “Make a sandwich” tells us the goal. Card B gives the exact steps. Computers need the steps, not your hopes.
feedback.incorrect: “Make a sandwich” is just a goal without steps. Look for the card that gives the exact actions.

content.prompt: You want a glass of water. Put the actions in the correct order:

items.text: Put the glass on the table.

content.explanation: Some actions depend on prior actions. You must have and fill a container before drinking from it.

feedback.correct: Clean sequence! You have to prepare the glass and pour the water before you can drink.
feedback.incorrect: Something happened too early. Look at what you need before you can do that step.

content.question:
Look at this sequence:
1. Get a cup.
2. Put water in the cup.
3. Drink the cup.

Which instruction is the problem?
content.explanation: The assistant followed every word faithfully. The failure happened because the third instruction asked for the wrong action.

feedback.correct: You don't drink the cup—you drink what is inside it. The instructions were followed; the problem was the instruction itself.
feedback.incorrect: Steps 1 and 2 prepare the cup cleanly. Look at what step 3 asks you to physically consume.

content.question: Which single change fixes the sequence?

options.text: Change “Drink the cup” to “Drink the water.”
Move “Drink the cup” to the first step.

content.explanation: When an outcome is wrong, isolate and change only the specific instruction that caused the issue.

feedback.correct: Nice. One instruction was wrong. We changed only that instruction.
feedback.incorrect: We don't need to delete setup steps or add extra cups. Change only the instruction that had the wrong target.

content.prompt: The assistant needs to make a glass of orange juice. Arrange the actions:

items.text: Put the glass on the table.
Put orange juice in the glass.

content.explanation: The container must be set up and filled before drinking can occur.

feedback.correct: Spot on! The container and liquid must exist in place before you can drink.
feedback.incorrect: Check what is required first. You cannot pour or drink without having the glass ready.

content.question: Why can't “Drink the juice” go first?

options.text: The juice isn't in the glass yet.
Drinking must always be the first step.
The table has to be empty.

content.explanation: An action cannot succeed if the prerequisite it relies on has not happened.

feedback.correct: Exactly. An action cannot succeed if the thing it needs hasn't been created yet.
feedback.incorrect: Think about physical reality: you cannot drink something that isn't in the glass yet.

content.prompt: Complete the instruction with the exact item needed:
content.template: To brush your teeth, first get your {{item}}.

blanks.hint: What specific tool do you hold to clean teeth?

content.explanation: Instructions must explicitly name the exact item required.

feedback.correct: Right. The instruction must identify the exact tool needed.
feedback.incorrect: The assistant needs the specific tool for brushing teeth. Pick 'toothbrush' from the Word Bank.

content.prompt: Choose the exact item to put on the toothbrush:

blanks.hint: What cleaning paste goes on the brush?

content.explanation: Exact naming prevents the assistant from using the wrong item.

feedback.correct: Exact instructions leave no room for guessing.

content.title: Three Things to Remember
takeaways: Computers follow instructions literally: If an instruction is vague or wrong, the computer doesn't magically repair your intention.
Order matters: Some actions only make sense after another action has already happened.
A correct execution can still produce a bad result: If the instruction is wrong, perfect obedience doesn't save you.
nextSteps: Don't ask, “What did I mean?” Ask, “What exactly did I tell it to do?”
